name: Synthetic Dialogue Profiling
description: Analyzes the structural rhythm and syntactic completeness of written conversations to distinguish between organic human dialogue and rigid, algorithmic 'tennis match' exchanges.
mechanism: Authentic human dialogue is messy. People interrupt each other, speak in grammatically broken fragments, use implicit references ('deixis'), and frequently leave thoughts unfinished, relying heavily on shared context and non-verbal cues. Large Language Models, however, are fundamentally designed to generate complete, parsed, and self-contained logical statements. When tasked with writing dialogue, AI typically produces 'tennis match' conversations: perfectly alternating turns where each speaker delivers a grammatically flawless, multi-clause sentence that explicitly states their internal thoughts and perfectly addresses the previous speaker's point. There is zero conversational overlap, no syntactic fragmentation, and a pathological avoidance of ambiguity. This NLP method analyzes the structure of quotation blocks, measuring the length, syntactic completeness, and dependency trees of the spoken lines. An abnormally high rate of complete sentences, coupled with an absence of conversational repairs (stuttering, self-correction) and fragments, strongly flags the dialogue as a machine-generated simulation.
useCase: Detecting AI authorship in creative writing, novels, screenplays, and narrative essays where the characters speak like perfectly rational textbook algorithms rather than flawed human beings.
strengths:
• Highly effective against standard prompt attacks, as getting an AI to consistently hallucinate realistic 'messy' dialogue requires extensive, highly specific constraints.
• Leverages deep syntactic tree analysis rather than simple vocabulary checks, making it robust against synonym-swapping.
• Excellent for analyzing long-form fiction and creative writing assignments.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives in highly formalized human writing styles, such as stage plays written in a classical, declamatory style (e.g., Shakespearean or Socratic dialogues).
• Ineffective on text that does not contain explicit conversational exchanges (quotation marks or script formats).
• Requires a substantial amount of dialogue context to establish a statistically significant pattern of 'tennis match' exchanges.
parameters:
Analysis: Quotation Block Extraction & Syntactic Parse Tree Evaluation
Metric: Conversational Fragmentation Ratio & Turn-Taking Uniformity
Output: 0-100 Synthetic Exchange (Tennis Match Dialogue) Score
accuracy: High — 80-90% within creative contexts. An incredibly reliable marker of machine generation in narrative fiction, as LLMs fundamentally lack the lived experience required to replicate human conversational chaos.

references.title: Biber, D. et al. (1999). Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English. Pearson Education.
Clark, H. H. (1996). Using Language. Cambridge University Press.
